problems.description: 6 naming-convention violations (snake_case/PascalCase/UPPER_CASE) across app.py, test_notification_server.py, and transport.py drop the convention score to 0.73.
Cognitive complexity +64 with 3 new SonarQube smells across the +252 added lines indicates convoluted control flow in the new server/transport code.
A threading.RLock guards the client registry inside a single-threaded asyncio event loop — unnecessary and signals confusion about the concurrency model.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: entry point (app.py), server class (notification_server.py), and transport module
Zero new bugs and zero duplication per SonarQube
Well-formed async lifecycle (start/stop, connection cleanup in finally) with type hints on public signatures
Complete, testable notification-server implementation delivered in a greenfield session
commit_reviews.summary: Solid greenfield notification-server build with clean module separation and zero new bugs, but naming-convention violations, +64 cognitive complexity, and 3 smells introduce moderate technical debt.

problems.description: Dual bookkeeping via two inverse maps (channels and _client_channels) must be updated symmetrically in _set_subscription and the disconnect path; a single subscription registry (or helper owning both directions) would reduce drift risk.

HTTP routing for /channels/{name}/subscribers relies on string startswith/endswith + manual unquote rather than a structured route; fine for two endpoints but will not scale to more routes without a dispatcher.

subscribe/unsubscribe with a missing or non-string channel returns silently (no error surfaced to the client), which may mask protocol misuse; cognitive complexity +13 reflects the added branching in _handle_message.

strengths: New subscribe/unsubscribe logic reuses the existing message wire format, RLock discipline, and async gather pattern rather than inventing new ones.
message() signature is backward compatible (channel is optional), so existing broadcast/direct/system callers are unaffected.
Channel-scoped broadcast restricts fanout to subscribers only, avoiding a global broadcast storm as channel count grows.
Disconnect handler cleans up both _client_channels and channels maps consistently, avoiding subscriber leaks.
HTTP introspection endpoints (/channels, /channels/{name}/subscribers) mirror the existing /health handler style, with proper 404 handling and URL decoding via unquote.
Tests added alongside the feature.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted, convention-following feature addition that extends the notification server with channel subscriptions using existing patterns and lock discipline, adding only minor maintainability surface from dual-inverse state bookkeeping.

problems.description: _store_message performs synchronous SQLite I/O directly on the asyncio event loop (called from async _publish/broadcast/send_direct), blocking the loop; connection is opened without WAL mode or an index on messages.
_redis_listener swallows every non-cancellation exception with a bare 'except Exception: pass', so a JSON decode error or Redis failure silently drops messages with no logging.
Redis pub/sub fan-out and SQLite persistence are folded directly into NotificationServer rather than extracted, inflating cognitive complexity by +46 in one class.
Redis listener polls get_message with timeout=1.0 in a busy loop instead of blocking on a single receive, adding idle wakeups.

Convention score 0.73 is driven by violations in app.py, test_notification_server.py, and transport.py, none of which appear in the visible diff; the added code itself is consistently snake_case/PascalCase — flagged as a discrepancy between measurement and the commit's own changes.

strengths: Graceful degradation: optional redis import, 0.5s ping timeout, and local _deliver fallback keep the server functional without Redis.
Correct asyncio hygiene: CancelledError re-raised in _redis_listener and task cancelled in _stop_redis.
_close_resource robustly handles both aclose() and close() for pubsub/client cleanup.
Env-driven configuration via REDIS_URL and DATABASE_URL with sensible defaults.
Reuses existing message() and _deliver helpers rather than duplicating wire-format logic.
commit_reviews.summary: A reasonable integration commit (Redis fan-out + SQLite persistence with graceful fallback) that respects existing patterns and conventions, but the +46 cognitive complexity, blocking DB writes on the event loop, and silent exception swallowing in the Redis listener introduce moderate technical debt.

problems.description: Transport abstraction is speculative: TRANSPORT env var accepts only 'websocket' and raises ValueError otherwise, so the seam has exactly one implementation (YAGNI until a second backend lands)
SonarQube cognitive complexity +194 and +10 smells on this refactor — moving connection/delivery logic into the transport layer increased complexity despite the cleaner separation
Type narrowing regressed: self.clients changed from dict[str, ServerConnection] to dict[str, Any] and _on_connect takes connection: Any, losing the concrete type information
getattr(self.transport, 'port', self.websocket_port) uses duck-typing instead of a declared property on BaseTransport, weakening the interface contract
New transport.py introduces module-level constants that are not UPPER_CASE, contributing to the 0.73 convention score
Pre-existing snake_case/PascalCase/constant violations in app.py and test_notification_server.py appear in the convention report but are not clearly addressed by this commit

strengths: Zero new bugs and no duplication added per SonarQube

problems.description: Only the rate-limit path has a test; the new /history endpoint and the TTL cleanup loop have no test coverage.
Cleanup interval is hardcoded (asyncio.sleep(3600)) rather than configurable alongside message_ttl_days.
In-memory _local_rate_limits fallback grows with unique client/bucket keys and is only pruned lazily on each rate-limit check.
Cognitive complexity +18 comes from extending the HTTP dispatch elif chain with the /history branch; consistent with the existing pattern but trending complex.

strengths: Rate limiter with Redis incr/expire plus in-process fallback mirrors the existing dual-mode (Redis-or-local) design throughout the class
Config via constructor arg with env-var fallback (_env_int) matches the established server configuration pattern
Async cleanup task lifecycle mirrors _redis_task: created in start(), cancelled and gathered in stop()
TTL cleanup prevents unbounded messages-table growth; /history uses parameterized SQL with LIMIT+1 pagination (has_more)
Net quality improves: 0 new bugs, 2 smells removed, no code duplication
commit_reviews.summary: Architecturally well-integrated commit that adds rate limiting, message TTL cleanup, and a paginated /history endpoint while faithfully following existing patterns; the measured 0.73 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in app.py and transport.py (unrelated to this diff), so the commit's own additions are judged convention-clean, though test coverage lags behind the two new features.

compounding_issues: Dual connection bookkeeping: after S4's transport refactor, both NotificationServer.clients and WebSocketTransport._connections track the same connections, creating two sources of truth that must be kept in sync.

Redundant connect/disconnect wiring in WebSocketTransport._register: on_connect/_on_connect and on_disconnect/_on_disconnect are both called for the same event, leaving ambiguous ownership between injected callbacks and overridden methods.

S1's per-client registry under a single threading.RLock carried through S2's channel maps (_client_channels) and survived the S4 refactor, so the server retains client-side state that the transport abstraction was meant to encapsulate.

S5's rate limiter counts every inbound message type (including subscribe/unsubscribe and direct) against one per-minute bucket and relies on an unbounded in-process dict fallback when Redis is absent.
key_decisions: Greenfield in S1 as an async WebSocket notification server with broadcast/direct/system wire types plus a bare HTTP health endpoint
Channel/subscription model in S2 with channel-scoped broadcasts and HTTP introspection endpoints (/channels, /channels/.../subscribers)
Redis pub/sub with graceful degradation plus SQLite message persistence in S3 to enable cross-instance delivery and message history
Transport abstraction in S4 (BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport behind a TRANSPORT env seam) decoupling connection handling from routing logic
Cross-cutting hardening in S5: Redis-backed rate limiting with local fallback, message TTL cleanup loop, and paginated /history retrieval
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. Session 1 delivered a clean, single-purpose server with solid basics (unique IDs, locking, 4 tests). Session 2 added a coherent channel/subscription feature set with introspection endpoints and matching tests. Session 3 integrated Redis pub/sub and SQLite persistence with graceful degradation when Redis is unavailable, laying the storage groundwork later sessions reused. Session 4 was a genuine architectural improvement rather than churn: extraction of a transport abstraction reduced coupling and broadened extensibility, though it introduced dual connection tracking and redundant callback wiring at the boundary. Session 5 capped the arc with rate limiting, TTL cleanup, and a paginated history endpoint that reuses S3's persistence. Test coverage grew from 4 to 10 tests across all sessions, and all 10 pass at the final commit; the only blemish is the residual bookkeeping overlap introduced by the refactor.
story_review.summary: A logically sequenced, upward-trending story that progressed from a minimal WebSocket server to a transport-abstracted, Redis-integrated, rate-limited notification system with clean feature reuse, marred only by mild state-duplication fallout from the Session 4 refactor.
